items.followUp: What is the difference between an incubation period and the duration of an illness?

rubric.why: Identifies the interval as beginning when infection occurs and ending when symptoms appear.
rubric.description: States when the incubation period begins and ends.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining it as the time from infection or entry of a pathogen until symptoms appear.

rubric.why: Clarifies that the period ends with the appearance of symptoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explicitly stating that symptoms have not yet appeared during this period.

modelAnswer: The incubation period is the time between a pathogen entering the body (infection) and the appearance of the first symptoms.
During this period, the infected person may not yet show symptoms.

items.followUp: Define communicable disease and give one example.

rubric.why: Gives observable structural features of smooth muscle fibres.
rubric.description: Describes smooth muscle fibres as spindle-shaped and/or having a single nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct structural feature, such as spindle shape or one nucleus per fibre.

rubric.why: Adds a distinguishing feature, location, or mode of action of smooth muscles.
rubric.description: States that smooth muscles lack striations, are involuntary, or occur in the walls of organs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct distinguishing feature or location.

modelAnswer: Observe a prepared smooth-muscle slide under a microscope: the fibres are spindle-shaped, each with a single nucleus.
They have no striations and contract involuntarily; they are found, for example, in the walls of the alimentary canal.

items.followUp: What is facilitated diffusion? Give one example.

rubric.why: Defines active transport as requiring energy to move substances against their concentration gradient.
rubric.description: States that active transport uses energy to move substances against the concentration gradient.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both energy use and movement against the gradient.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of active transport.
rubric.description: Gives an example, such as mineral-ion uptake by root hairs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any correct example.

modelAnswer: Active transport is the movement of substances across a cell membrane against their concentration gradient, using energy (ATP).
For example, root-hair cells use active transport to absorb mineral ions from the soil.

items.followUp: State two ways biodiversity benefits people or ecosystems.

rubric.why: Recognizes a valid ecological or human-use benefit of biodiversity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid benefit, such as ecosystem stability, food, medicines, or raw materials.

rubric.description: Gives a second, different importance of biodiversity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another valid benefit; do not award twice for repeating the same point.

modelAnswer: Biodiversity helps maintain the stability of ecosystems.
It also provides useful resources such as food, medicines, and raw materials.

items.followUp: Name two human activities that can cause habitat loss.

rubric.why: Identifies a major threat that destroys or reduces natural habitats.
rubric.description: Names one major threat to biodiversity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid threat, such as habitat destruction, deforestation, or land conversion.

rubric.why: Requires a second distinct major threat.
rubric.description: Names a second major threat to biodiversity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another valid threat; do not award twice for the same threat.

modelAnswer: Major threats to biodiversity include habitat destruction, such as deforestation and conversion of land for human use.
Other major threats include overexploitation, pollution, invasive species, and climate change.

items.followUp: Why are viruses described as being at the boundary between living and non-living things?

rubric.why: Identifies the absence of cellular organization in viruses.
rubric.description: States that viruses are acellular or lack cellular structure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that viruses are not made of cells.

rubric.why: Explains that viruses depend on a host cell for reproduction and are inactive outside it.
rubric.description: States that viruses reproduce only inside host cells or are inactive outside a host.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the host-dependent nature of viral reproduction.

modelAnswer: Viruses are excluded from the five-kingdom classification because they are acellular and lack cellular structure.
They do not reproduce independently; they replicate only inside a living host cell and remain inactive outside it.

items.followUp: How does apoptosis help maintain normal tissues?

rubric.why: Identifies apoptosis as controlled, programmed cell death.
rubric.description: Defines apoptosis as programmed cell death.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying apoptosis as controlled or programmed cell death.

rubric.why: Explains its role in removing damaged or unnecessary cells and maintaining healthy tissue.
rubric.description: States that apoptosis removes damaged or unwanted cells or prevents harmful cell growth.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct role in eliminating damaged/unneeded cells or limiting uncontrolled growth.

modelAnswer: It removes damaged or unwanted cells, helping maintain healthy tissues and preventing the continued growth of abnormal cells.

items.followUp: Give one example of regeneration in an animal.

rubric.why: Describes regeneration as replacement or regrowth of lost or damaged body parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that lost or damaged body parts are replaced or regrown.

rubric.why: Explains the cellular process or gives a valid example of regeneration.
rubric.description: Mentions cell division and differentiation, or gives a correct example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing cells dividing and differentiating, or for an example such as planaria regrowing from a fragment.

modelAnswer: Regeneration occurs when cells at a damaged or lost part divide and then differentiate to form the required tissues.
For example, a planarian can regenerate a complete organism from a body fragment.
